answer: The highest growth phase between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE occurred in the 15th century BCE (1500–1401 BCE), with a mean pollen_grate_100 of +0.001889, followed closely by the 14th century BCE (1400–1301 BCE, mean +0.001114). Together, the 15th–14th centuries BCE (1500–1301 BCE) constitute the highest growth phase of the period. This is corroborated by the KDE archaeological growth rate (g_all_mean = +0.002829 in the 1500s BCE, the highest of any century) and by the largest positive change in capital Z-scores (ΔZ = +0.68) in the 1400s BCE.

payload.hypothesis: The highest growth phase of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE occurred in the 15th century BCE (1500–1401 BCE), as measured by the mean percentage change of the 100-year smoothed pollen openness score (pollen_grate_100 = +0.001889). The 14th century BCE (1400–1301 BCE) constitutes the second phase of this growth episode (pollen_grate_100 = +0.001114). The two centuries together (1500–1301 BCE) represent the peak growth phase, corroborated by the maximum KDE archaeological growth rate (g_all_mean = +0.002829 in the 1500s BCE) and the largest positive shift in total capital Z-scores (ΔZ = +0.68 in the 1400s BCE).
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded time_series_data.csv (3601 rows, 1-yr resolution, CE -4100 to -500), capital.csv (39 rows, 100-yr bins, BCE 4300-500), and pollen_openness_score (4084 rows, 1-yr, CE -702 to -4785). 2) Extracted the 2000-1100 BCE window (CE -2000 to -1100, 901 rows). 3) Binned into standard centuries (N-th c. BCE = CE -(N*100) to CE -(N*100-1)), yielding 9 full centuries + 1 boundary year. 4) Computed mean and median pollen_grate_100 per century as the primary growth metric. 5) Ran sensitivity checks: ±10 yr boundary shift, mean vs median ranking, cumulative sum. 6) Cross-referenced top 3 centuries with g_all_mean (KDE growth) and capital Z-score totals (mean of 12 Z-variables, 100-yr bins). 7) Confirmed ranking stability across all checks.
